description:
I'm a 16-year-old Grade 11 student based in Abu Dhabi, UAE, with experience developing AI-powered mobile and web applications. I'm passionate about artificial intelligence, software development, and solving real-world problems through technology.

For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, I plan to build an innovative, functional project using AI and NASA data. I'm focused on creating a high-quality solution and may collaborate with one friend.
summary: Mission Pulse AI helps astronauts interpret their own health readings and decide what to check next during a mission. In a simulated Artemis II case, the app compares three nights of sleep with the crew member’s personal baseline and flags a missing reading for follow-up. The crew can test a maintenance change, see when it conflicts with a fixed briefing, and choose a slot that gives them eight hours of scheduled rest instead of six. Mission Pulse also records follow-up measurements beside the originals and exports a handover for crew or flight surgeon review. The prototype uses published NASA mission records and clearly labeled synthetic crew data.
details:
Astronauts on long missions need to assess changes in their own health and balance follow-up with fixed work. Mission Pulse groups health check-ins, personal baselines and the mission schedule in one browser app. It tracks sleep, pulse, blood oxygen, blood pressure, glucose, temperature and breathing rate. Each flagged value shows the comparison rule and relevant measurement context. The app marks missing readings explicitly and records a recheck beside the original reading.

In the Artemis II rehearsal, the app rejects a maintenance slot that overlaps the 09:00 briefing. Moving the work to 07:00–09:00 increases the scheduled rest window from six to eight hours. The crew can export a local handover draft with the evidence, the proposed change and NASA sources. The ISS rehearsal shows a simulated pulse of 106 bpm after exercise alongside a 64 bpm resting recheck. The Apollo 17 rehearsal illustrates missing baseline data and multiple vital-sign flags.

NASA’s Artemis II agenda informs the sleep-window scenario. NASA’s ISS sleep brief and Apollo records provide historical context. Crew measurements, decisions and schedules used in the drills are synthetic. Guidance focuses on checking data quality, repeating readings and preparing a review. It is intended for simulation and review.

I built the dashboard in React and TypeScript with Vite and hosted the public demo on Lovable. The public app stores rehearsal data in the browser and answers supported typed questions from its current records. I used OpenAI Codex to assist with planning, writing and reviewing code, testing, synthetic data and submission materials. Lovable assisted with the import and deployment. The optional local prototype uses OpenJarvis for model-backed replies and actions, and Faster Whisper for transcription.
